title: Four motives
hook: wrongdoing comes from desire, hate, delusion and fear

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sigala's bow. Your line: each direction has a face in it. Today closes a week, and the Buddha asks Sigala to look at why people go wrong.
screen: `EACH DIRECTION HAS A FACE IN IT.`

segments.voice: A referee calls a foul on the visiting team that wasn't a foul. Why? Maybe he likes the home team. Maybe he can't stand the visiting coach. Maybe he just didn't see it clearly. Or maybe forty thousand people were screaming, and he was afraid. Four possible reasons, and the same bad call. Before the Buddha explains the six directions to Sigala, he names exactly these four.
screen: `A BAD CALL.` → `LIKING, DISLIKE, CONFUSION, FEAR.` → `THE SAME FOUL.`

segments.voice: In the Sigalovada the Buddha says a wise person does no evil from four motives: desire, hate, delusion, fear. The Pali calls them agati, wrong courses, four ways the mind goes off the road. Desire bends you toward what you want or who you like. Hate bends you against someone. Delusion means you simply don't see clearly. And fear bends you toward whatever keeps you safe. Look at that last one. Elsewhere the discourses name three roots of harm: greed, hate and delusion. This list adds fear. Plenty of harm isn't done out of malice at all. It's done by someone afraid to speak up, or afraid to lose a job, or afraid of a crowd. Then the Buddha puts it in verse. Whoever goes against the Dhamma from desire, hate, fear or delusion, his good name fades, like the moon in the waning half of the month. Whoever doesn't, his good name grows, like the moon in the waxing half. One shrinking, one filling, and the verse is about a young householder's good name. The same four turn up in the monastic rules: a monk chosen to share out food or lodging must be one who doesn't follow them. And the week behind us: chosen, not born; what I trust; well proclaimed; the marks of kindness; a protective chant; six directions; and now four reasons a good person might still make a bad call.
screen: `AGATI: FOUR WRONG COURSES.` · `DESIRE, HATE, DELUSION, FEAR.` · `FEAR IS ON THE LIST.` · `THE WANING MOON, THE WAXING MOON.` · then, large: `FOUR MOTIVES.`

segments.voice: Recall one recent decision you're not proud of; small is fine, a sharp word, a corner cut, a silence when you should have spoken. Hold it gently and ask which motive was at work: wanting something, disliking someone, not seeing clearly, or fear. Don't judge yourself; just name it, the way you'd name a bird you spotted, and rest with the breath.
Four motives. In DN 31: desire, hate, delusion and fear, the four wrong courses that lead good people into bad acts. Today's word.
Your line: desire, hate, delusion, or fear? A good name waxes or wanes with the answer. A week done; see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers present the four agati as a checklist for fairness, and the monastic rules name them as the biases a monk who shares out food or lodging must avoid.

fork.setup: a referee makes a bad call because forty thousand fans are screaming at him. which of the four motives is at work?
fork.reveal: fear. the Sigalovada names it alongside desire, hate and delusion as a reason good people do wrong.

original.note: Pali agati: wrong course, a way off the road. the four are chanda, dosa, moha and bhaya.

trapdoor: what you thought: wrongdoing comes from bad intentions.
what it means: the Sigalovada names four motives, and one of them is simply fear.
what a scholar hears: the four agati (chanda, dosa, moha, bhaya) recur in the Anguttara (e.g. AN 4.17–20) and the Vinaya names them as the biases an officer of the community must avoid.

chat.says: Why does that Buddhist list of wrong motives include fear? Isn't fear just normal?
options: Fear is normal, but it bends choices; much harm comes from being afraid to speak.
Fear is the worst wrong of all, so a good person must never feel afraid.
Because fear is the root of greed, hate and delusion, the other three.
chat.meaning: DN 31 lists desire, hate, delusion and fear as four wrong courses; fear is there because plenty of harm is done by people who are afraid.
